2 Abstract We present the protocol and data analysis toolbox for Multi-Contact 4C (MC-4C), a new proximity ligation method tailored to study the higher-order chromatin contact patterns of selected genomic sites. Conventional chromosome conformation capture (3C) methods fragment proximity ligation products for efficient analysis of pairwise DNA contacts. In contrast, MC-4C is designed to preserve and collect large concatemers of proximity ligated fragments for long molecule sequencing on Oxford Nanopore or Pacific Biosciences platforms, thus allowing study of multi-way chromatin interactions. By inverse PCR with primers specific for a fragment of interest (the viewpoint) and DNA size selection, sequencing is selectively targeted to thousands of different complex interactions containing this viewpoint. A tailored statistical analysis toolbox employing data-intrinsic background models then discerns whether contacts between more than two regulatory sequences are mutually exclusive or, conversely, simultaneously happening at chromatin hubs. The entire procedure can be completed in two weeks and requires access to a third generation sequencing platform. Introduction Development of MC-4C Chromatin conformation capture (3C) methods 1,2, employ in situ DNA digestion and proximity ligation to detect contacting DNA fragments and investigate chromosome topologies inside cells. Most protocols also include a formaldehyde crosslinking step prior to digestion to preserve spatial proximity, although fixation seems not strictly necessary 3. Current high-throughput 3C variant methods include Hi-C (for unbiased and untargeted genome-wide contact analysis) 4, 4C and capture-C technologies (for unbiased analysis of contacts made by one or more selected genomic sites of interest) 5–7 and ChIA-PET and Hi-ChIP (for contact analysis between sites occupied by a protein of interest)8,9. All these methods use Illumina short read sequencing for massively parallel analysis of pairwise DNA contacts, which for optimal results requires trimming the ligation products to sizes far below one thousand base pairs. A limitation of all methods measuring pairwise contacts is that when three or more elements are identified to interact in a cell population, it remains unclear whether this occurs simultaneously in the same cell or in a pairwise fashion in different cells or at different time points. Pairwise methods thus also fail to identify if interactions occur (i) in a cooperative fashion (forming prefered multi-way contacts, or hubs, on the same allele), (ii) in an uncoordinated (random) fashion, or (iii) in a competitive fashion, forming contacts that are mutually

3 exclusive on single alleles. Increasingly, enhancers, gene promoters and CTCF bound sequences are found engaged in contact networks with multiple other local regulatory sequences. Such contacts between individual regulatory sequences and genes, only to be discovered by targeted high-resolution 3C approaches and in very deeply sequenced Hi-C datasets, are functionally the most meaningful chromatin interactions with the potential to directly impact gene expression. They usually take place within the context of topologically associated domains (TADs), chromosomal regions of on average 1 Mb in size that self-interact and thereby form the structural and functional units of chromosomes 10–12. MC-4C was developed to reach resolutions that allow study of such local functionally important contact networks and enable discerning whether regulatory sequences and genes spatially aggregate in chromatin hubs or, oppositely, compete with each other for contacts. In recent work, we showed that MC-4C can identify enhancer hubs, formed between the individual elements of a super enhancer and we demonstrated by MC-4C that some genes compete while others cooperate with each other for interaction with this enhancer hub. MC-4C further allowed demonstrating that CTCF-
bound boundaries of neighboring domains aggregate to form rosette-like chromatin structures in interphase cells. This phenomenon became even more apparent upon depletion of the cohesin-unloading factor WAPL, which made us propose that the boundary bouquets we observed are the consequence of ‘traffic jams’ of extruding cohesin molecules that collide into each other if not adequately removed by WAPL 13. Applications of MC-4C MC-4C can be applied to any genomic locus in any cell type or species, where it can uncover how local individual regulatory sequences and genes within a 120 kb to maximally 2 Mb genomic interval (explained below) spatially coordinate their action at the single allele level. The uncovering of these higher-order topological frameworks is expected to facilitate interpreting genotype-phenotype relationships. It can help, for example, to understand why certain regulatory sequences appear redundant while others seem crucial for proper gene expression. Besides regulatory interactions and hubs, we expect MC-4C to be instrumental for the uncovering of periodicity of chromatin folding, if existing in given genomic intervals and at given moments of the cell cycle. Finally, data generated by MC-4C should be extremely useful for the validation and optimization of current 3D genome modeling algorithms 14,15 that all rely on pairwise proximity ligation measurements to infer the higher-order topologies that MC-4C directly measures.

4 Comparison with other methods Recently, several breakthrough methodologies were developed to study multi-way chromatin contacts. One example is C-Walks (chromosomal walks) that employs serial dilution, fragmentation and barcoding of large proximity-ligation concatemers, followed by sequencing and in silico reconstruction of the ligation products 16. C-walks is an untargeted, genome-wide, method that randomly collects and identifies multi-way contacts from across the genome. It was used to investigate the spatial aggregation of intra- and inter-chromosomal regions inside so-called nuclear compartments and therefore essentially analyzes how TADs position themselves relative to each other in the cell nucleus. It was suggested that at this level of spatial organization, preferred multi-
way chromatin clustering is rare but may occur for example at polycomb bodies 16. Three-
way Hi-C contact analysis methods17, GAM (genome architecture mapping)18 and SPRITE (split-pool recognition of interactions by tag extension)19 are other novel untargeted, genome-wide methods for investigating chromatin clustering at the level of nuclear compartments. SPRITE uses a sophisticated barcoding system based on repeated pooling and splitting of crosslinked DNA ‘hairballs’ to uncover clustered DNA fragments from across the genomes of many cells and enabled uncovering hubs of inter-
chromosomal contacts at nucleoli and nuclear speckles 19. GAM is another orthogonal method that is not dependent on DNA digestion and ligation but that isolates and sequences the DNA content of many ultra-thin cryo-fixed nuclear slices for in silico analysis of favored spatial chromosome configurations. GAM also showed preferred multi-way clustering of intra- and inter-chromosomal regions dense in active genes and super enhancers18. While very elegant and insightful, none of these methods (currently) provides sufficient local coverage to study the important regulatory contact networks and intricate higher-
order topologies that are formed inside TADs. A recently developed targeted multi-
contact strategy, called Tri-C20, was designed to study this fine-scale level of 3D genome organisation and was shown to generate data and results similar to that obtained by MC-
4C. Tri-C uses biotinylated capture probes instead of inverse PCR methods to enrich for multi-way contacts centered on a viewpoint fragment of interest, in a protocol that requires minimal PCR amplification. For efficient pull-down, the long proximity ligation products are first sheared to ~450 bp products prior to pulldown and Illumina paired-end sequencing is used to analyse the products (~50% contains multiple ligation junctions). The unique ends that are created by sonication serve as unique molecule identifiers (UMIs) for filtering out PCR duplicates. Tri-C can be scaled to analyse millions of multi-
way contacts, of which the great majority will be 3-way. In comparison, with MC-4C we typically analyze roughly ten thousand different micro-topologies per single Nanopore

5 MinION run. Since these are larger, more complex, ligation products, this adds up to analyzing nearly hundred thousand different local contacts per experiment. A distinct feature of MC-4C is the analysis package that comes with the protocol, which we developed to enable robust interpretation of three-way interactions. Recognizing that pairwise contact frequencies in a region of interest are unique for each cell-type of interest and must be considered to interpret multi-way contact frequencies, we designed a statistical method that does not compare multi-way contact profiles from different tissues, but evaluates each dataset independently. Based on a data intrinsic statistical comparison of observed over a thousand background-predicted multi-contact frequencies, z-scores are assigned to co-occur frequencies.This enables robust distinction between cooperative, random and competitive multi-way interactions between regulatory sequences and genes in a locus of interest, as we have shown recently13. Experimental Design MC-4C is based on 4C technology, a ‘one-versus-all’ contact analysis method that we previously developed to search the genome in an unbiased fashion for sequences contacting a selected DNA fragment of interest5,21. Both methods are based on 3C1 and involve circularization of proximity ligation products followed by inverse PCR with primers specific for the target fragment of interest, to amplify and analyze the DNA fragments its alleles were ligated to in the cell population. Where the original 4C protocol aims to minimize the sizes of circles that need to be amplified by PCR, MC-4C is modified such that it aims to best preserve the long concatemers with multiple DNA fragments ligated to the fragment of interest. To generate and analyse such long PCR-
amplified concatemers, the procedure was tailored as follows and combined with long-
read single molecule sequencing on third-generation sequencing platforms like Oxford Nanopore Sequencing or Pacific Biosciences. As in most 4C and Hi-C protocols, four-cutter restriction enzymes were used for in situ digestion of formaldehyde crosslinked DNA. This results in small DNA fragments (average size 250 bp) that, as a consequence of formaldehyde fixation, often stick together in ‘hairballs’ with multiple other crosslinked DNA fragments. Subsequent in situ ligation fuses these ‘hairball’ DNA fragments together, yielding large concatemers of ligated fragments. We further process these large DNA molecules with a secondary six-
cutter restriction enzyme to obtain concatemers with sticky-ends (for efficient ligation-
mediated circularization) and of a size (average 4 kb) that will harbor many ligation partners but can still be amplified by PCR with inversely oriented primers that bind to the restriction fragment of interest (the viewpoint). It is essential that this viewpoint-fragment is i) of a sufficient size to accommodate two primers and a guide RNA (gRNA) binding

6 site in-between the primers; usually between 200 and 500bp; ii) is overlapping or at least in close (<1Kb) linear proximity to the genomic element for which 3-way interactions are to be studied (i.e. overlapping with a promoter, enhancer or bound CTCF site) and iii) does not contain any internal secondary restriction (i.e. HindIII) sites. For the viewpoint fragment, a set of inverse primers must be developed that bind uniquely and are positioned >50bp from the DpnII restriction sites. Allowing some spacing between the restriction sites and the primer binding sites facilitates viewpoint detection after long-read sequencing. We recommend testing the PCR primers on a small batch of MC-4C template, to assure that they yield products in the 2-5 Kb range. If this is not the case, their efficiency can be optimized with alternative annealing temperature and the addition of DMSO and/or MgCl2 to the PCR reaction, although satisfying results are often faster obtained by simply ordering a new set of primers elsewhere on the same viewpoint. PCR amplification is performed using a highly processive polymerase in a reaction with an extension time that enables replication of the long concatemers. In such reaction, rolling-circle PCRs prioritize amplification of shorter DNA circles. This, we noticed, causes an overrepresentation of small products having only the target fragment of interest with or without its natural neighbor fragments on the linear chromosome. They account for the majority of reads but are not informative for genome topology studies. To eliminate them and target sequencing to informative concatemers, we included an in-vitro Cas9 digestion step prior to PCR that simultaneously cuts the target fragment of interest (in between the inversely oriented PCR primer binding sites) and its two neighbor fragments (see Fig. 1b and c). gRNAs can be designed using several available online tools (described in the “guide RNA design and validation” section ). We routinely first test their effectiveness on genomic DNA or a small amount of MC-4C template prior to their use on bulk MC-4C template. For this, we design a PCR across the Cas9 cleavage target site and measure the in vitro digestion efficiency of Cas9 at this site by quantitative PCR (qPCR). Prior to sequencing, products are size selected and sequenced on a long-read single molecule sequencing platform. To process, analyze and interpret this new type of sequencing data, a custom pipeline was designed that stringently removes PCR duplicates and is able to identify and quantify multi-way interaction profiles. Importantly, we have developed an analysis pipeline that compares observed three-way interaction frequencies to data-predicted background contact frequencies, allowing data-intrinsic statistical analysis of complex interaction profiles.

7 Fig. 1: schematic overview. a. Summary of the the MC-4C protocol: chromatin is first crosslinked using formaldehyde, and then digested using a restriction enzyme (DpnII). Subsequently, fragments in close physical proximity are ligated in situ. The DNA concatemers are then isolated and re-digested with a 6-cutter restriction enzyme. Subsequent ligation results in circularization of the template concatemers. A viewpoint-
specific Cas9 digestion is then applied to avoid amplification of frequent background products and rollin-circle PCR’s. Next a viewpoint-specific inverse PCR is performed. b. Primer and gRNA design overview. For a selected viewpoint fragment, a set of inverse primers is designed with approximately 50bp in-between the primer binding site and the

8 first digestion sites. Three gRNA’s are then designed to cut in-between the inverse primers, and in each of the “neighbouring” fragments. c. Rationale of cutting the “neighbouring” fragments. A frequent by-product of proximity ligations are viewpoint-
fragment self-ligation, and undigested or re-ligated VP-neighbour fragments. These take up a large proportion of the PCR product and sequencing capacity. When the three gRNA’s are successfully applied, such by-products are fragmented, and can no longer yield PCR product, while informative ligations between the viewpoint and non-
neighboring fragments are left intact. Expertise needed to implement the protocol The preparation of MC-4C template is very similar to our published protocols for the preparation of 4C template6,21, but has been optimized by the use of magnetic beads for DNA purification. Thus, the use of (commercially available or homemade) magnetic separators is required. The final steps of the protocol, size selection and long read single molecule sequencing, require a specialized gel-separating device and an Oxford Nanopore or Pacific Biosciences sequencing device. Limitations A limitation of the MC-4C protocol is the high numbers of cells that are required. To accommodate for the loss of material that occurs at various steps of the protocol, and for the fact that the majority of the PCR product is below the ideal >1.5Kb size range, we generally pool 96 individual PCR reactions for each viewpoint, with a total of 100ng of template per PCR reaction. Thus, about 20ug of template is required per viewpoint (where conventional 4C only requires 800ng). Out of 2*10^7 cells we routinely generate 60ug of template, allowing for 3 MC-4C analyses. For most tissue culture cells obtaining 2*10^7 cells is not difficult, but for certain primary tissues or FACS sorted cell populations this may be prohibitive amounts of material. Further, MC-4C only provides meaningful insights into higher order topologies for genomic intervals within a given size range. At the lower size limit we recommend not to consider regions smaller than 120kb: our current analysis strategy pools restriction fragments into a standard number of 200 bins across the region of interest, no matter the size of this region. Below 120 kb the sizes of these bins become smaller than 600bp, i.e. often erroneously implying a resolution below the restriction fragment size. At the upper size limit relevant data interpretation requires a minimum amount of multi-way contacts with distal sites, which relies on

9 sequence depth. In practice, this limits analysis to contacts within TADs, or between a few adjacent TADs within 1-2 Mb (see further below). We further notice that, as compared to Illumina sequencing, the sequencing throughput provided by Nanopore and PacBio platforms is still limited (but improving rapidly), and indexing strategies are not yet routine practice. As a result, we currently only run single MC-4C experiments per flow-cell. When different viewpoints are used, the primer sequence should be traceable though and can serve as an inherent barcode, allowing pooling of multiple samples in a single run. Incubate for 15 minutes on ice. Troubleshooting: For some cell types, longer incubation is required for digestion to be effective. This is likely due to a more sturdy cell membrane. Data pre-processing In this section, we will describe the MC-4C pipeline which is designed to facilitate data processing, analysis and interpretation of sequenced MC-4C experiment. It should be noted that this pipeline is under continuous development which adds new functionalities or enhances the existing ones. Therefore, we recommend the user to refer to the github repository of MC-4C pipeline (https://github.com/aallahyar/mc4c_py) to access the latest version of the MC-4C pipeline as well as the corresponding manual which describes the newly added features or enhancements in the pipeline. 26 Note: Selection of a Region of Interest (ROI) requires careful consideration. This is because ROI width has an important role in several parts of the MC-4C data processing pipeline. Initially, the ROI discerns far-cis fragments that can be used as UMIs for duplication removal procedure. Additionally, it identifies “informative” reads (i.e reads with more than one fragments in the ROI) that can be used in multi-contact analysis. Finally, the multi-contact analysis is performed by splitting the ROI into 200 non-
overlapping and equally-spaced bins. The user is strongly advised to consider the following suggestions when determining the coordinates for ROI: ● The viewpoint should always be included in the ROI. This is important as exclusion of viewpoint can change the expected distribution of fragments in the ROI which in turn results in unreliable z-scores calculated in the multi-contact analysis. ● If an experiment is expected to investigate interactions within a given TAD, the ROI should encompass the TAD boundaries and a few dozen kilobases of flanking sequences, as done previously 13. ● The ROI size should not be smaller than 120Kb when MC-4C library is prepared using DpnII restriction enzyme as the first cutter. Smaller ROIs will result in a bin width less than 600bp (i.e. 120Kb / 200) which is close to expected minimum resolution of such MC-4C experiment (for human or mouse genomes). ● The ROI can be larger if interactions between TAD boundaries are investigated as done previously 13. However, considering the expected coverage of a (4bp cutter) MC-4C experiment, the ROI should not be larger than 2Mb as sufficient coverage is required for a reliable multi-contact analysis and further interpretation of results (further discussed below).

37 Sequencing saturation level: Insufficient complexity (i.e. diversity of reads amplified) in an MC-4C library can result in low yield of unique reads. To assess the obtained complexity of an MC-4C experiment, the seqSaturation command in QC module can be used. This command produces two panels (see Fig. 9). Initially this command investigates the sequencing saturation by downsampling reads in a given MC-4C experiment and plotting the number of reads versus the number of unique reads (see Fig. 9 left panel). If the plotted line reaches a plateau (ie. sequencing more reads does not yield more unique reads), the user can conclude that the current library is saturated. Additionally, this command calculates a UMI duplicity score (The frequency of an observed UMI divided by the total number of informative reads, multiplied by 1*10^5). By plotting top 100 UMI duplicity scores one can estimate the library complexity. The average duplicity score of all UMIs can be used to the same effect, and is typically below 20. Generally, a MC-4C dataset with sufficient diversity of UMIs should have an average duplicity score below 20. Refer to Troubleshooting for further actions if the UMI duplicity score is substantially higher than 20. a. b. 39 Association analysis of a single site of interest (atVpSoi) This analysis is performed when the user is investigating whether the interaction propensity of the viewpoint and a given bin within the Region Of Interest (ROI) changes when a Site Of Interest (SOI) is present in the same read. This analysis is implemented in vpSOI command within the analysis module. Fig. 9. shows an example plot produced by this command. VP-SOI analysis: This analysis is devised to investigate the three-way associations between view point, SOI and any given third partner in the ROI. The corresponding details for this analysis are described extensively in our original publication 13. In summary, we compare the chance of three-way interaction between the viewpoint, the SOI and a given site as the third partner (i.e. the positive set), to a background profile that reflects the three-way interactions of the viewpoint and the same site in absence of the SOI (i.e. the negative set). To estimate the background, we randomly

40 sample a number of reads from the negative set equal to the number of reads in the positive set. We randomly remove a fragment from each sampled read in the negative set to compensate for the SOI fragment present in all reads in the positive set. This random sampling is repeated 1000x to generate an average background profile and corresponding standard deviation. The VP-SOI contact profile is then compared to the background profile, and a z-score is calculated. When the positive profile is higher than the background, a genomic region is more likely to interact with the viewpoint in the presence of the SOI. A positive profile similar to the background profile indicates that such region is equally likely to interact with the viewpoint with or without presence of the SOI. When the positive profile is lower than the background, a region is less likely to contact the viewpoint when it is interacting with the SOI. *figure adapted from Allahyar et al. 13. 43 Troubleshooting Pre sequencing troubleshooting 1) Difficulties obtaining single cell suspensions: The ability to obtain a single-cell suspension is crucial for homogenous crosslinking, but differs between cell or tissue types. In some cases more stringent treatment is needed, for example by using tissue homogenizers, collagenase treatment or cell straining devices. Spotting a small aliquot of the sample on a microscope slide and viewing the cells under a standard microscope can give an impression of the suspension homogeneity. 2) Poor digestion efficiency: Digestion efficiency varies between cell types, and may be inadequate using the standard procedure described here. The first course of action in such cases is to add more restriction enzyme (usually 100U DpnII), and to incubate at 37˚C for 3 hours. Repeat the digestion control step, and compare the result with the earlier digestion control (See Fig. 2c). If no improvement is visible, the problem is likely due to suboptimal permeabilization. In such cases it may help to recollect the cells by centrifugation and repeating steps 3-10 of the template preparation protocol. Extension of the lysis incubation time (step 3) can also improve digestion efficiency, if incomplete digestions are a recurring problem with a particular cell-type. 3) Poor ligation efficiency: If ligation fails to show a clear upwards shift of the template on an agarose gel, the troubleshooting is similar to that of poor digestions: first course of action is to add 40 units of Ligase enzyme, and fresh ATP to a final concentration of 1mM and re-incubating at 16˚C overnight. If this does not improve ligation efficiency, repeat step 1-7 of the template preparation protocol to improve cell permeability, and then repeat steps 14 and 15. 4) Poor gRNA performance: In some cases gRNAs fail to digest their target DNA, for this reason we recommend first testing them in a small scale on genomic DNA. If gRNAs do not perform well, we recommend designing a different gRNA on the same target region. In cases where gRNAs perform well on gDNA, but not on MC-4C template we have seen improved performance when the MC-4C template was purified using a Qiagen PCR purification kit. However, this does negatively influence the template yield. In this case, split 40 𝜇g’s of template over four Eppendorf tubes and purify each aliquot with one column so as not to exceed the maximum loading capacity of the columns.

44 5) PCR optimization: It is essential that MC-4C PCR yields PCR products >1500 bp (see Fig. 2d), if this is not the case then further PCR optimization is required. Adjusting primers and annealing temperatures may make a significant difference in large product yield, but in some cases shifting the viewpoint to a neighbouring fragment is necessary. In other cases the MC-4C template may still contain smaller fragments that are favored in the PCR reaction, these can be excluded to some extent by re-doing the 0.5x-0.6x AMPure XP purification. If strong bands are still visible in the PCR smear, as seen in the example in Fig. 2d, this indicates that one or multiple gRNAs did not work. If the bands are below the 1.5Kb size-selection threshold, they are still excluded by the pippin size selection, so if the smear does have a significant amount of material >1.5Kb, then it can still be sequenced. However, if enough template is available we recommend troubleshooting the gRNA performance (see troubleshooting #4). Post sequencing troubleshooting: 1) Poor size selection: In the MC-4C protocol a 1.5-8kb interval is used for selecting MC-4C PCR product prior to sequencing. However, after sequencing, we sometimes observed smaller reads. This could be caused by poor size selection procedure. One can assess the efficiency of size selection by inspecting the read size distribution of sequenced library using QC module (see Data quality control section for details). An efficient size selection should result in a normal distribution of reads sizes in the 1.5-8kb interval. An example of such a distribution is given in Fig. 13a. Improper size selection can result in a library that still contains many small reads. An experiment where small reads were unexpectedly sequenced is shown in Fig. 13b. Running the MC-4C pipeline on a sample with poor size selection, will result in excessive read filtering, as a high percentage of reads will contain <3 fragments. However, the remainder of reads can still be analysed as usual.
